title: Hf: Dielectric-swap kit converts legacy DRAM fabs to FeRAM
idea: Depreciated 2x-3x nm DRAM fabs swap their ZrO2 capacitor dielectric for Si- or Zr-doped ferroelectric HfO2 in the same cylinders, add plate-line drivers and new sense timing, and make 1T1C FeRAM; Hf comes from U.S. nuclear-zirconium refining byproduct.
why: Non-volatile, refresh-free DRAM-class memory from fabs with near-zero new capital.

title: Magnify periodicity: mask-free interference lithography for memory arrays
idea: Memory arrays are perfect gratings, so print them with a ~$300k four-beam 193 nm laser interference exposure in one flash per wafer, pitch-split by self-aligned quadruple patterning, repeated for 4 array tiers; all irregular periphery goes on a cheap CMOS chiplet hybrid-bonded on top.
why: Removes EUV scanners and masks from the array (litho ~30-40% of wafer cost and most capex); ~10x cheaper array processing times 4 stacked tiers targets ~100x lower cost per GB.

title: Phone LPDDR packages reballed onto CXL bridge cards
idea: Po: every phone is a memory mine. Recyclers desolder LPDDR4X/5 packages from end-of-life phones (hot-gas rework plus automated reballing), test them on a fixture, and mount 16-32 of them on a CXL Type-3 card whose controller bridges the LPDDR protocol and masks per-package defects with a remap table.
why: >1B phones a year reach end of life holding 4-12 GB each; recovering even 10% yields billions of GB of capacity-tier memory for cold pages with zero wafer starts; attacks cost per bit and scarce capacity.

title: Cuban mechanic's almendron: keep old DDR4 alive behind CXL
idea: Havana mechanics keep 1950s cars running with improvised parts. In the same spirit, low-cost CXL Type-3 bridge cards each host 8-16 retired DDR4 RDIMMs and give new DDR5 servers a second-life capacity tier. The controller adds chipkill-class ECC and runs the DDR4 at reduced speed so it lasts longer.
why: Reuse supply: hyperscalers retire tens of millions of DDR4 DIMMs a year; reusing them could displace 10-20% of new DDR5 purchases for capacity-bound workloads, at ~150 ns extra latency.

title: Mechanical vibration: ultrasonic debonding harvests DRAM dies from retired modules
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration: retired DIMMs and phone boards pass through cryogenic shock plus ultrasonic delamination that releases BGA packages without thermal stress; packages are re-balled, retested and rebinned for CXL memory expanders.
why: Reuse/recycling: tens of exabytes of DDR4 retire yearly; even 10% recovery adds meaningful capacity-tier supply.

title: Shipping-container micro-fabs printing DRAM arrays by nanoimprint
idea: Ideal: a fab that fits anywhere and costs as much as a house. Closest achievable: 40-ft containerized minienvironments use jet-and-flash nanoimprint for the dense, regular array layers (honeycomb capacitor holes, bitlines) and dry ArF for periphery, ganged into $200-500M micro-fab clusters.
why: Capital intensity, EUV avoidance and U.S. manufacturability: claimed ~10x less capex per wafer-start module; imprint defectivity is the main risk.

title: Tire-retreading: re-package harvested die into 125 C packages
idea: Like retreading a sound tire casing, laser and plasma decapsulation strips the consumer-grade mold compound and bond wires from harvested DRAM, die that pass a 125 C retention screen are re-bumped and re-packaged in high-Tg, low-chloride mold compound rated for 10 years at 125 C.
why: Upgrades the good fraction of e-waste die into the scarce, premium automotive/industrial grade, adding a recycled supply of high-temperature parts.

title: Magnify reuse: mine e-waste DRAM with a polyglot CXL controller
idea: Robotic lines desolder LPDDR/DDR3/DDR4 packages from discarded phones and PCs, test them, and mount them on carrier boards behind a 'polyglot' CXL controller that speaks every legacy protocol, absorbs mixed speeds and adds strong ECC, producing pooled memory sleds.
why: Input cost is near scrap value; at ~$0.05-0.15/GB automated handling, memory comes out ~100x cheaper than new contract DRAM, and billions of discarded GB per year rival annual production.

title: Biologist's self-assembly: block copolymers draw 5 nm cells
idea: Cells build structures by self-assembly. High-chi silicon-containing block copolymers on sparse ArF guide patterns define a 10 nm-pitch hexagonal array of vertical nanowire access transistors, each with an oxide-semiconductor storage node instead of a capacitor. Spin-coat and anneal from U.S. chemical suppliers replace 5-7 EUV layers.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 4F^2 at F=5 nm vs 6F^2 at 12 nm is ~8.6x; with periphery under the array, ~10x/mm^2. Spin-and-bake costs far less than EUV, so wafer cost stays flat; DSA defectivity is the big risk.

title: Right-to-reuse mandate: socketed memory plus module deposit refund
idea: Worse: solder all LPDDR to the board so the memory dies with the laptop or phone. Flip: require socketed CAMM2/LPCAMM-class modules in PCs and servers above a price threshold, plus a $2-5 per-module deposit refunded when modules reach certified refurbishers.
why: Moves recovered consumer memory from near zero to a majority of units, roughly doubling DRAM bit-life and cutting new-wafer demand; lowers capital and scarce-resource intensity per useful bit-year.

title: Planarize nothing: area-selective growth eliminates CMP slurry water
idea: Reverse blanket-then-polish into growing only where needed: area-selective ALD/CVD with inhibitor monolayers fills trenches and contacts from the bottom up to the target height. That removes CMP, its slurry and the post-CMP clean.
why: CMP and post-CMP cleans are a large share of fab UPW. Removing several CMP steps cuts that share >10x and also eliminates slurry waste.

title: Cold-grade bins: sell retention-reject dies to cryo and immersion racks
idea: Extreme user: 4 K quantum-control racks and LN2- or oil-immersed AI pods, where DRAM retention rises by orders of magnitude. Fabs create a priced 'cold-grade' SKU from dies that fail 64 ms retention at 85 C but pass at 45 C or below, sold with a contractual maximum case temperature to immersion-cooled racks that hold DIMMs at 30-40 C.
why: Retention-tail fallout (fact 3) is scrapped or downbinned today; reclaiming 2-5% of wafer output as a priced bin adds bit supply with zero new capex.

title: Linux Foundation model for open U.S. DRAM periphery IP
idea: Adapted from the Linux Foundation: pooled university, startup and federal money maintains open-source, silicon-proven sense amps, row decoders, charge pumps, DDR5/LPDDR5 PHYs and BIST engines for a U.S. DRAM PDK, under patent non-assertion pledges.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (Fact 7) and expensive IP; open, proven blocks cut a new U.S. entrant's design cost and time ~50% and grow the domestic supplier base (capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Williams Tube 2.0: Field-Emitter Arrays From Abandoned FED Display Lines
idea: Revive the 1947 Williams tube (bits as charge spots on a dielectric written and read by an electron beam) using the field-emission-display tooling Candescent and Sony abandoned: each microtip emitter addresses a 1-4 um patch of unpatterned charge-storage film, read back by secondary-emission sensing, so cell density is set by beam focus rather than lithography.
why: Litho-bound scaling and capital: the storage film needs no patterning or EUV, and mothballed display vacuum lines supply the emitter arrays.

title: Eliminate phantom orders: privacy-preserving demand ledger kills the bullwhip
idea: Eliminate double- and triple-ordering: OEMs, distributors and makers post orders into a secure-multiparty-computation ledger that de-duplicates the same end demand arriving through multiple channels, so producers see true demand without revealing customer secrets.
why: Shortage panics inflate orders ~20-40% and starve small buyers; truthful demand redirects existing supply to real users and prevents the following glut.

title: Eliminate single-product fabs: dual-qualified NAND/DRAM swing lines
idea: Eliminate the fixed product mix: pre-qualify shared tool sets (much of litho, etch and deposition overlaps) with both DRAM and NAND recipes and reserve slots for DRAM-only tools, allowing a 3-6-month swing to DRAM when NAND is in glut.
why: Turns existing NAND overcapacity into DRAM supply in months instead of 3-5 years.

title: Eliminate single-sourced footprints: universal multi-vendor DRAM board footprint
idea: Eliminate board respins when one DRAM part disappears: publish an open reference footprint and routing that accepts LPDDR4X, DDR4 x16 and LPDDR5 packages via option resistors and a small interposer, validated on three SoC platforms; ~$400k.
why: Lets designers buy whatever DRAM is in stock, widening the effective supply pool.

title: Active interposers doubling as SRAM memory under accelerators
idea: Worse: pay for 2,500 mm2 silicon interposers that only carry wires. Flip: build interposers on depreciated 65/40 nm lines with SRAM arrays filling the area under and between chiplets, giving accelerators ~100-300 MB of static near-memory.
why: Zero refresh, made from silicon area customers already pay for.

title: Grandparents' fabs: depreciated lines make thin array layers for bonding
idea: Retirees still work, and cheaply. Fully depreciated 300 mm fabs (28-40 nm) make array-only wafers with just 3 ArF masks and no periphery. These are thinned to 5 um and hybrid-bonded 16 deep onto one leading-edge wafer that carries all sense amps and decoders.
why: Toward the 10x constraint: 16 array layers at ~0.6x areal density each is ~10x bits per footprint. Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost and is gone in written-off fabs, so the full stack costs ~1.5x one conventional wafer for 10x the bits (~6x lower $/bit). This misses strict same-cost, but it makes a new business for old fabs.

title: Carrier freeze-out at 77 K lets old fabs build tiny-capacitor memory pools
idea: At liquid-nitrogen temperature junction and subthreshold leakage fall >10^6x, so a 1 fF planar capacitor on a 65 nm transistor holds data for minutes. Build cryogenic memory pools in LN2-immersed racks from cells made on depreciated 65-40 nm lines.
why: Bypasses the charge wall and refresh and uses idle mature capacity; LN2 is cheap and domestically abundant.

title: Mixed-vendor DIMMs harmonized via per-DRAM addressability trims
idea: Box[Source=qualified dies from any vendor x Transform=per-die timing and Vref trims via DDR5 PDA mode registers set by the RCD at boot x Integration=standard RDIMM x Owner=module maker]: build modules from whichever qualified dies are available and let the buffer program each die's offsets.
why: Supply fungibility: modules need not wait for one vendor's dies, smoothing allocation shortages; interface unchanged.

title: No wafer at all: roll-to-roll steel-foil memory with drum nanoimprint
idea: Forced limit: no discrete substrates. Stainless-steel foil gets a planarizing dielectric, then sputtered oxide-semiconductor and drum-nanoimprinted gain-cell layers in a continuous web line.
why: Capital intensity: web processing cuts tool cost per m2 by about 10x versus batch wafers; foil is cheap and plentiful.

title: Self-assembled honeycomb: block-copolymer holes for storage-node capacitors
idea: Cylinder-forming PS-b-PMMA packs hexagonally on its own, the same honeycomb DRAM capacitor arrays use. Coarse i-line guide posts register the polymer, which self-assembles 4-9x denser hole arrays. Those holes are etched into the mold oxide as storage nodes.
why: Litho capital: replaces 1-2 EUV or quad-patterning layers with spin-coat, bake and RIE, all nanofab-standard.

title: Zn: Tellurium-free zinc-antimonide phase-change memory from Idaho antimony
idea: Use Zn-Sb phase-change alloys (fast, high crystallization temperature) instead of GeSbTe in crosspoint storage-class memory, sourcing antimony from Idaho's Stibnite deposit.
why: Te is a ~500 t/yr byproduct and Ge is China-concentrated; Zn-Sb gives non-volatile memory from abundant-to-domestic elements.

title: Substitute ballroom cleanrooms with sealed mini-environment tool chains
idea: Swap ISO-class-1 ballroom cleanrooms for tools linked by sealed FOUP/overhead transport and local mini-environments, so the building is an ordinary industrial shed.
why: Cleanroom building and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab capex and much of its energy; targets ~15-25% capex cut and faster construction.

title: Federated university fab relay with baton-passed wafer lots
idea: Fuse a network of university and national-lab 200/300mm cleanrooms with a MOSIS-style shuttle. Each site certifies 1-2 module steps (implant, capacitor ALD, metallization), and lots travel in sealed nitrogen FOUPs on a scheduled courier loop.
why: Uses $10B+ of stranded, underused U.S. tool sets to make pilot and defense DRAM and to train the workforce, with no new fab.

title: Slow the depreciation clock: 15-year frozen-node vintage memory
idea: Commit a fully depreciated 1x/1y-nm DRAM line to a frozen node for 15 years, with products (heritage DDR5, LPDDR5 capacity parts) designed for that node, sold on a cash-cost-plus basis instead of retiring tools after 5 years.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost; a depreciation-free line cuts cost per bit ~2x and keeps capacity in the market instead of scrapping it.

title: Richmond fab clause: reversionary option keeps closed fabs warm
idea: When Qimonda's 300 mm fab near Richmond, Virginia closed in 2009, its tools were sold off and the U.S. lost a DRAM fab for good. Fix: every subsidized fab carries a reversionary option, so on closure the government can buy the cleanroom, utilities and tools at depreciated book value, keep them at minimum burn (purge, utilities, skeleton crew), and lease them to a new operator.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: restarting a warm shell takes ~12-18 months and ~30% of greenfield capex, versus 3-5 years and $15B+ for a new fab.

title: Cuckoo strategy: oxide memory panels made in idle LCD fabs
idea: Cuckoos raise their young in other birds' nests. Overbuilt Gen-8.5/10.5 display fabs already make IGZO TFT backplanes on huge glass; they run memory arrays on panels that are diced into tiles and bonded to silicon periphery chiplets.
why: Taps depreciated, underused capacity of millions of m2 per year, at ~100x lower cost per area than silicon wafers.

title: Convert U.S. hard-disk head wafer fabs to memory chiplet production
idea: Adapted from HDD recording-head fabs in the U.S., which run fine lithography, ion milling and magnetic-stack deposition on AlTiC wafers: as disk volumes shrink, retool them to make SOT-MRAM-class or oxide DRAM-class memory chiplets on the same deposition, milling and metrology tools.
why: Brings existing U.S. cleanrooms and skilled staff into memory without greenfield capex, adding domestic capacity within 1-2 years (capital intensity, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Bank-fused salvage dies sold as partial-capacity SKUs
idea: Combine DRAM yield binning with CPU-style core harvesting. Dies whose failures exceed the redundancy budget have whole banks or bank groups e-fused off and are sold as 12 Gb, or as 3/4-capacity parts, with an SPD-declared address map that controllers already support.
why: Turns 3-8% of scrapped die per wafer into sellable bits, which lifts effective wafer output a few percent with no extra capex.

title: Prior action: central EUV hub ships pre-patterned wafers to one-mask spokes
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: a single EUV-equipped hub performs all critical array patterning, then ships wafers to distributed U.S. spoke fabs that finish deposition, implants and BEOL using DUV plus exactly one customization mask.
why: EUV single-supplier chokepoint: concentrates EUV use while multiplying finishing capacity cheaply.

title: Retention-binned dies shipped with mandated fine-granularity refresh
idea: Box[Source=dies failing 32 ms retention test x Transform=bin and mark as short-retention SKU x Integration=standard DIMM, SPD flags 2x refresh x Owner=DRAM maker]: dies that miss retention spec but pass at doubled refresh are sold as a discounted SKU, and BIOS reads the SPD flag and enables DDR5's 2x refresh rate.
why: Turns retention-tail scrap into supply (~1-3% more good bits per wafer) at ~1-3% bandwidth cost; no interface change.

title: Prefabricated copy-exact fab pods cut build time to 18 months
idea: Box[Fab=factory-built cleanroom and utility modules x Scale=10k wafers/month pods x Owner=modular fab builder x Finance=pod-by-pod project finance]: build DRAM capacity in identical shippable modules (cleanroom, sub-fab, utilities) that bolt together, so capacity is added in increments.
why: Capital and time: an estimated 18 vs 36-60 months to first wafer, smaller financing tranches; output is standard DDR5/HBM.

title: Magnify the wafer: 450 mm reserved for DRAM alone
idea: Revive the shelved 450 mm tool set as a single-process DRAM consortium (one standard cell, one recipe, U.S.-hosted pilot line) because DRAM is the most uniform high-volume product; each wafer pass yields 2.25x the dies for roughly 1.4x the tool cost.
why: Cost per bit ~20-30% lower and fewer scarce EUV-hours per bit; the first 450 mm line becomes a U.S. manufacturing anchor.

title: Molten-salt electrorefining reclaims tungsten and ruthenium from spent sputter targets
idea: Planar targets are scrapped at ~30-40% utilization and chamber shields collect metal. A regional refinery anodically dissolves W/Ru/Ta in a fluoride-chloride melt where ions migrate and plate as 5N metal, sold back to target makers under buy-back contracts.
why: Creates domestic secondary tungsten supply from the ~60% of target metal now wasted.

title: ETA10's cryo bet revisited: LN2-cooled legacy-node memory pools
idea: ETA Systems' liquid-nitrogen-cooled CMOS supercomputer (ETA10) died in 1989 from cost and timing, not physics. Fix with cryo for memory only: 180 nm DRAM dies at 77 K leak orders of magnitude less (refresh nearly disappears) and switch ~1.5-2x faster, so pooled LN2-cooled shelves of old-node memory approach modern latency and idle power.
why: Makes depreciated-fab memory performance-competitive (refresh cost near zero, faster transistors); density stays low and cooling overhead is the risk, so it suits pooled capacity tiers.

title: Copy-approximately licensing lets new fabs run looser process windows
idea: Inverts 'process transfer must be copy-exact': a vendor licenses its DRAM flow to new second-source fabs with widened control limits, where tool-matching gaps raise cell faults to within 1%, so the fab ships before full matching is done.
why: Time to capacity and U.S. manufacturability: cuts process transfer from ~2 years to months and lets mixed tool fleets qualify.

title: Submariner's closed loop: recapture every liter of fab helium
idea: Submarines recycle everything. Fit each etch and deposition chamber's backside-cooling and leak-check helium lines with local recovery (pump-exhaust capture plus membrane and cryogenic purification) that returns 6N helium to a fab-wide loop.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar offline): 85-95% recapture cuts a fab's helium purchases ~10x and removes a shutdown risk.

title: IBM MXT rebuilt at 180 nm: cold-page compressing module buffer
idea: IBM's Memory eXpansion Technology (2000) doubled server memory with hardware compression but was dropped for its added latency once DRAM became cheap. Fix: a 180 nm buffer chip on the module compresses only cold pages during idle cycles (base-delta and zero-page codecs small enough for 1990s gate budgets), while hot pages stay uncompressed, so most accesses pay no penalty.
why: ~1.5-2x effective capacity on existing DIMMs; at 4x bit prices, a few-dollar 180 nm chip is cheaper than buying the bits.

title: Ni: Electroplated permalloy racetrack memory from HDD write-pole plating lines
idea: Electroplate NiFe nanowires into deep trenches like HDD write poles to form vertical racetrack shift registers holding 10-100 domain-wall bits read by one sensor at the top.
why: Electroplating costs ~1/10 the capex of vacuum deposition and gives many non-volatile bits per footprint.

title: Loom-woven flex interposers: polyimide-copper bolts replacing silicon CoWoS
idea: Weave a multilayer polyimide/copper redistribution 'cloth' on a carrier wafer by spin-coat, i-line lithography and semi-additive plating at 2 um line/space, then release it. Like woven tape, it can be cut to length to wire 1024-bit HBM-class buses between memory and logic with no silicon interposer.
why: HBM interposer tax and the CoWoS capacity chokepoint: silicon interposer area goes to zero, and the line costs ~10x less. Spinner, aligner and plating bath suffice.

title: Pottery wheel: 3D-print crucibles from polysilicon-byproduct synthetic silica
idea: Random stimulus 'pottery wheel' -> shape clay, then fire it. SiCl4 byproduct from polysilicon plants is converted to synthetic fumed silica, robocast or SLA-printed into crucible green bodies, and sintered to bubble-free fused silica.
why: Takes Spruce Pine natural HPQ out of the loop using a waste stream US polysilicon makers already have; secures DRAM wafer supply.

title: Flip the hierarchy: 3D NAND as main memory, DRAM as cache
idea: Reverse DRAM's place in the hierarchy: capacity-bound workloads (embedding tables, KV-cache spill, vector databases) run on memory-semantic SLC 3D NAND behind a CXL controller. A small DRAM cache sits in front, so bulk capacity comes from 200+ layer NAND.
why: 3D NAND gives roughly 10x+ more bits per wafer than DRAM, so water and capex per GB of capacity fall ~10x. DRAM wafers are saved for latency-critical use.

title: Co-site fabs on domestic helium fields with closed-loop recapture
idea: Po: the fab sits on a helium well. New DRAM fabs are sited at U.S. helium-bearing gas fields (Kansas/Texas Hugoton, Wyoming) with a dedicated cryogenic extraction plant, and every helium-using tool (backside cooling, leak check, purge) exhausts into a membrane-plus-PSA recapture loop.
why: Removes exposure to the Qatar outage (~30% of supply) and recaptures ~80-90% of fab helium; attacks scarce-resource intensity.

title: Reverberating-circuit acoustic delay-line memory in BAW filter fabs
idea: Brains hold short-term memory as activity reverberating around neural loops. Bits circulate as GHz acoustic pulses in recirculating BAW/SAW delay loops with regenerating amplifiers, made in U.S. RF-filter fabs (AlN/ScAlN) as streaming buffers for sequential AI data.
why: Uses non-DRAM RF capacity with no capacitor or refresh; low density, so it suits FIFO buffers that offload DRAM bandwidth.

title: LTPO display fabs printing complementary-TFT SRAM on glass
idea: Worse: leave Gen-8 display fabs idle while chip fabs are full. Flip: use the LTPS p-type plus IGZO n-type complementary TFTs already made for LTPO phone displays to build static 6T SRAM arrays on large glass panels, diced into memory tiles.
why: Static, so zero refresh; glass area costs orders of magnitude less per cm2 than silicon and opens an independent supply chain. Speed is ~100 ns-class, so it suits big buffers.

title: Helium reserve sell-off answered: closed-loop helium recapture per tool
idea: The 1996 Helium Privatization Act sold off the U.S. federal helium reserve, and Qatar's outage now starves fabs. Fix: fit recapture skids to every helium-using tool (backside wafer cooling in etch and implant, purge, leak check) that collect helium from the exhaust, purify it with membranes and pressure-swing adsorption, and feed it back to the tool.
why: Scarce resources: ~80-90% less helium bought per wafer, turning a geopolitical chokepoint into a small top-up.

title: Bit Purchase Agreements turn DRAM fabs into financeable infrastructure
idea: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost, so the cost of capital is a first-order term in $/bit. Copy the solar PPA: hyperscalers sign 10-year take-or-pay contracts for Gb/month at a fixed price, letting a new fab be project-financed largely with ~6-7% debt instead of a ~12-15% equity-weighted WACC.
why: Capital intensity and cost per bit: dropping WACC from ~13% to ~7% cuts the annualized capital charge ~30%, i.e. ~15% off cost per bit, and funds fabs that equity markets refuse at cycle peaks.

title: Child counting on fingers: 4-bit gain cells multiply existing fabs
idea: A child counts past ten by using more fingers per hand. Each non-destructive gain cell stores 16 current levels, read by a shared 4-bit flash ADC per 64 bitlines with per-row reference cells, and 3 tiers are bonded. A fabless memory-IP startup licenses it so existing DRAM fabs make ~4x the bits per wafer without new tools.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 4 bits/cell times 3 tiers is ~12x bits/mm^2. Multi-level sensing adds ~10% periphery while wafer cost stays put; level margin against leakage drift is the risk.

title: Capacitorless gain-cell memory on idle U.S. 22-28 nm logic lines
idea: The charge wall is a capacitor problem; a 3T gain cell stores charge on a transistor gate and amplifies it locally, needing no special capacitor process. Run gain-cell memory dies on underused U.S. 22-28 nm FD-SOI logic lines, using reverse back-bias to push leakage down for ms-class retention, accepting ~3-4x DRAM cell area.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: zero new fab capex and immediate capacity for buffer and cache-tier memory from existing domestic lines.

title: Transit Buy America ramp applied to federal data-center memory
idea: Adapted from FTA Buy America rules that ramped U.S. content in rail cars: memory in federally funded data centers and AI programs must rise from 10% to 70% U.S.-made content (wafer, assembly and test) over 8 years on a published schedule.
why: Gives domestic fabs a predictable demand base worth several EB per year, enough to justify capex, and counts wafers and packaging, not just final assembly (U.S. manufacturability).

title: HBM stacks ship with one weak die, lifting stack yield
idea: Inverts 'one bad die kills the whole HBM stack': the base die runs codes across its stack so stacks containing a die with up to 1% faulty cells (often from thinning or TSV stress) still ship.
why: HBM TSV tax: stack yield is down 20-30%; recovering half of failed stacks adds ~10-15% HBM output with no new wafers.

title: MRI-style closed-loop helium recovery on etch and litho tools
idea: Like hospital MRI and lab liquefiers that recapture boil-off, fit each electrostatic chuck backside-cooling and purge line with a recovery skid that compresses, membrane-purifies and returns helium to the fab loop.
why: Recovers >90% of fab helium use, insulating DRAM output from the Qatar outage and other helium shocks.

title: Tool-level cryogenic helium recapture closes the fab helium loop
idea: Helium is never consumed chemically in a fab; it is simply vented. Fit each wafer-cooling and purge exhaust with a membrane plus cryo-adsorption recovery skid that recompresses and repurifies to 5N, reaching >90% recycle.
why: Scarce resource: cuts fab helium draw ~10x while Qatar (~30% of supply) is offline; payback under 2 years at current prices.

title: Eliminate virgin tungsten: fab-scrap metals loop plus molybdenum swap
idea: Eliminate the mine-to-fab dependency: a US recovery loop refines spent W/Ta/Ru sputter targets (typically only ~30-40% consumed), chamber shields and CVD-W residue back to 6N purity, paired with qualified Mo wordline/contact substitution.
why: China holds ~80% of tungsten; ~60-70% of each target is recoverable, sharply reducing import exposure.

title: Copying: convert idle NAND fabs to capacitorless DRAM with one mask
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying: copy the NAND vertical-string flow and its tools wholesale, adding one mask that cuts each vertical channel into isolated floating-body segments operated as capacitorless gain-by-body-charge DRAM cells.
why: Supply: NAND overcapacity cycles become DRAM capacity; 3D density without new capacitor tooling (fact 2).

title: MRI-style closed-loop helium recovery across DRAM fabs
idea: Hospitals cut MRI helium loss ~90% with recondensers. Fabs, designed around the case of Qatar's supply offline, capture helium from wafer backside cooling, leak checks and purge lines with membrane-plus-cryo purifiers and recycle it on site.
why: Removes a chokepoint input (~30% of supply offline) and the tool downtime that shortages cause.

title: Fab-wide helium recapture loop with membrane and cryogenic polishing
idea: Scale jump from tool to fab: collect helium exhaust from chuck backside cooling, leak checking and purges into a fab-wide return header, then purify it with polymer membranes plus a small cryo-polisher and reinject it.
why: Qatar's ~30% of helium supply has been offline since March 2026. Recapturing 80-90% makes fab helium demand ~5-10x less exposed to that chokepoint.

title: Brewery-style recapture: closed-loop helium recovery inside every fab
idea: Breweries capture fermentation CO2 and reuse it. Fit fabs with point-of-use helium capture on etch-chuck backside cooling, litho stage cooling and leak-check exhausts, then purify back to 6N with membrane plus PSA and recompress on site.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline): 70-90% recovery cuts fab helium purchases 3-5x and de-risks wafer output.

title: Helium at zero for a year: recapture-and-substitute retrofit leasing
idea: Self-imposed limit: no helium deliveries. Leased retrofit kits recover helium from etch-chuck backside cooling and load-locks with membrane and cryogenic recovery (>90%), and switch tolerant chucks to hydrogen or argon backside gas. They are priced per wafer, not as capex.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: keeps fabs running through the Qatar helium outage (about 30% of supply) and cuts helium per wafer by about 10x.

title: Orphan-IP rescue fund relaunching thyristor static RAM
idea: Worse: let dead startups' memory IP, such as T-RAM thyristor cells, rot in patent portfolios. Flip: a fund buys orphan memory IP and relaunches thyristor RAM, a bistable negative-differential-resistance cell that holds state statically, on spare foundry SOI capacity.
why: No refresh at roughly 10-15F2 versus ~120F2 for 6T SRAM; revives a proven concept without new invention.

title: Archaeologist excavates know-how: rehire retired DRAM process veterans
idea: Treat process know-how as buried artifacts. A startup recruits retired DRAM integration engineers (Qimonda Richmond, Elpida and Micron Manassas alumni) into a 'reconstruction' team, digitizes their recipe notebooks, and rebuilds a 30-40 nm DRAM flow in 18 months instead of 5 years of R&D.
why: The know-how chokepoint: tacit process knowledge, more than tools, is the biggest barrier to entry; this cuts years off time-to-yield for a U.S. entrant.

title: Nanoimprint the periodic cell array, keep EUV for periphery
idea: Inverts 'every critical DRAM layer needs EUV': because the cell array is a near-perfect periodic lattice, pattern it with nanoimprint masters replicated from one e-beam write, and use EUV or 193i only for irregular periphery layers.
why: EUV single supplier and capex: removes 3-5 EUV exposures per wafer; litho capex per wafer start could fall 25-35%.

title: C: Coconut-carbon supercaps turn harvested DIMMs into persistent memory
idea: Retrofit kits pair second-life DIMMs with activated-carbon supercapacitors (coconut-shell carbon) plus a small NAND and controller that saves the DRAM image on power loss, sold as an Optane-replacement persistent tier.
why: Makes reused DRAM non-volatile and more valuable, improving harvest economics; no lithium or cobalt.

title: Substitute Chinese tungsten wordlines with Colorado molybdenum wordlines
idea: Swap CVD-W buried wordlines and contacts for ALD/CVD molybdenum sourced from U.S. Climax/Henderson mines, with a domestic MoCl5/MoO2Cl2 precursor plant co-located with a DRAM fab.
why: Removes the ~80% China tungsten chokepoint; Mo needs no TiN barrier, so line resistance falls ~20-30% at the same footprint.

title: Molybdenum wordlines from MoO2Cl2 replacing WF6 tungsten
idea: Fuse chloride-precursor Mo ALD/CVD (MoO2Cl2 or MoCl5) with Colorado Climax/Henderson primary moly supply to replace WF6-deposited W in buried wordlines and contacts.
why: Kills two chokepoints in one move: fluorinated WF6 and the 80% China tungsten share. Lower Mo resistivity in thin lines also helps scaling.

title: Mo: Climax molybdenum replaces Chinese tungsten in DRAM wordlines
idea: Switch buried-wordline fill and bitline contacts from WF6-CVD tungsten to barrierless MoO2Cl2/MoCl5-CVD molybdenum under long-term offtake from Colorado's Climax and Henderson mines plus a U.S. precursor plant.
why: Removes most exposure to ~80% China tungsten supply; barrierless Mo also lowers narrow-line wordline RC ~20-30%.

title: Molybdenum wordlines from Colorado mines to sidestep Chinese tungsten
idea: Ideal: DRAM made only of domestic elements. Closest achievable: replace tungsten buried wordlines and contacts with barrier-less ALD molybdenum, which has lower resistivity at thin dimensions, sourced from U.S. Climax/Henderson mines.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) plus ~20-30% lower wordline resistance.

title: Wine cellar: cool-grade binning of retention fallout for immersion-cooled racks
idea: Random stimulus 'wine cellar' -> some goods only keep when stored cold. Die that fail 64 ms retention at 85 C but pass at 45 C (leakage roughly halves per ~10 C) are sold as a JEDEC-style 'C-grade' only for immersion or cold-plate racks guaranteed below 45 C.
why: Recovers retention yield fallout as sellable bits (est. +2-5% bits per wafer) with zero new capex; attacks the leakage-tail/refresh wall by changing where the die live.

title: Hourly memory-capacity marketplace in colocation CXL pools
idea: Render farms, tax-season and quarter-close workloads are extreme users with offset peaks. Colos install CXL-switched DRAM pools and auction terabyte-hours to tenants, moving capacity between hosts in seconds.
why: Average DRAM utilization is ~40-60%; cross-tenant pooling toward 80% raises usable supply 1.3-1.6x.

title: IBM MXT Revival: Hardware Memory Compression Inside CXL Expanders
idea: Revive IBM's 2000 Memory eXpansion Technology (the Pinnacle controller: parallel LZ compression of 1 KB blocks into sectored storage with a decompressed-line cache) inside CXL Type-3 expander controllers, with a per-page translation table and an on-controller SRAM line cache so the OS simply sees about twice the capacity.
why: Usable supply: MXT measured ~2x on real server data; a 1.8-2.5x effective capacity on the pooled tier is equivalent to doubling DRAM output for that tier with zero new fab capacity.

title: Solar epitaxial lift-off: reusable porous-silicon donor for DRAM wafers
idea: Adapted from U.S. kerfless solar startups: grow 20-50 um epitaxial silicon on a porous-Si release layer over one CZ donor wafer, bond it to a U.S.-made polysilicon carrier, lift it off, and reuse the donor 10-20 times.
why: Cuts CZ crystal, quartz crucible, polysilicon and energy per DRAM wafer ~5-10x, so a few U.S. crystal pullers can feed a domestic fab base; the risk is epi defect density (scarce resources, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Si: Ion-cut donor reuse, one prime wafer feeds ten DRAM wafers
idea: Hydrogen-implant and cleave (Smart-Cut) the top 1-2 um of a prime CZ silicon wafer onto a cheap reclaimed or polysilicon carrier, then CMP and re-epi the donor and reuse it 10+ times, because DRAM arrays only use the top few microns.
why: Cuts CZ ingot growth, and so Spruce Pine quartz-crucible demand, per DRAM wafer by ~5-10x; turns a binary chokepoint into a small-volume one.

title: No silicon wafer: 300 mm glass wafers through existing BEOL lines
idea: Forced limit: no CZ silicon. Run oxide-semiconductor memory stacks on 300 mm borosilicate glass wafers in existing BEOL-only tool sets (all steps at or below 400 C). The process needs no crystal pulling, quartz crucibles or FEOL implant and anneal.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine crucible and CZ chokepoints, and substrate cost drops by 5-10x. It uses idle BEOL capacity at mature foundries.

title: Substitute EUV with nanoimprint for honeycomb capacitor array layers
idea: Swap EUV exposure on the perfectly periodic storage-node and landing-pad layers for nanoimprint lithography with e-beam-written masters, funded as a second-source litho program so array layers no longer depend on one EUV supplier.
why: Removes 2-3 of 5-7 EUV layers; NIL tools are ~1/3-1/5 the price of EUV with ~90% less power, cutting litho capex per wafer start by ~25%.

title: Self-expiring cache on retention-reject dies with write-time tags
idea: Worse: keep refreshing cache lines that will never be read again. Flip: each row carries a coarse write timestamp, and rows older than the die's measured retention count as cache misses refilled from flash or pooled memory, so weak-retention dies run with refresh off.
why: Zero refresh power, and dies that fail retention binning become usable supply.

title: Gutenberg's press: one 3D imprint stamps all 128 staircase steps
idea: Gutenberg replaced hand copying with a press. A 3D multi-level nanoimprint template, written once by e-beam, stamps all 128 staircase steps and tier contacts of a 3D DRAM stack in a single imprint, replacing ~30 litho/trim cycles. U.S. template shops and NIL tool vendors form the supply chain.
why: Meets the 10x constraint as a cost enabler: staircase and contacts are ~30-40% of a 3D memory wafer's cost, and collapsing them to one imprint lets a 128-tier 3D DRAM (~10x/mm^2) be built at about today's DRAM wafer cost.

title: OpenDRAM patent pool with FRAND royalties and reference PDK
idea: Ideal: DRAM know-how that is free to everyone. Closest achievable: gather licensable cell, sense-amp and buried-wordline patents from defunct-maker estates and universities into a FRAND pool bundled with an open reference PDK and test chips, so an entrant pays one fixed royalty instead of facing lawsuits.
why: Barrier to entry: removes multi-$B litigation risk and cuts years of design time for new makers.

title: National phone trade-in harvest of LPDDR into datacenter modules
idea: Time-and-scale mismatch: phones retire after ~3 years, but their LPDDR lasts 10+. Robots desolder LPDDR packages from billions of traded-in devices using nitrogen reflow, retest them, and rebuild them into CAMM/CXL modules for cloud tier-2 memory.
why: A flagship phone holds 8-16 GB. Recovering 10% of yearly smartphone retirements adds tens of exabytes, with no fab and no rare gases.

title: Photoconductive light-addressed wafer sort replaces probe cards for micro-fabs
idea: Add photoconductive test pads and on-die photodiode power harvesters; a projector flashes patterns that power and clock every die at once. Dies answer through modulated-reflection pads imaged by a camera, giving massively parallel contactless wafer test.
why: Probe cards ($1-3M each) and ATE are major capital barriers; contactless sort cuts test capex several-fold and avoids pad damage.

title: Parameter change: chilled-grade DRAM with one-mask on-die thermistor guarantee
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change: dies failing retention at 85 C but passing at 45 C ship as 'chilled grade' for liquid-cooled racks; one added mask adds a thin-film thermistor so the controller enforces the operating window and doubles refresh if exceeded.
why: Retention yield: leakage roughly halves per ~10 C, recovering a slice of dies scrapped today.

title: Ticket scalper: non-transferable allocation tokens to kill shortage double-ordering
idea: Random stimulus 'ticket scalper' -> named tickets stop scalping. During allocation, a clearinghouse issues non-transferable bit tokens tied to verified installed-base telemetry and past consumption, so buyers cannot double-order or hoard phantom inventory.
why: Bullwhip hoarding amplified the 2021 chip shortage; removing phantom orders frees est. 5-15% of shipped bits to real demand during spikes.

title: Array-only fabs: bond simple cell wafers to foundry-made periphery
idea: From first principles the array is a few periodic layers (wordline, bitline, capacitor) while periphery is generic logic. Split them: specialized array fabs with ~1/3 of a DRAM fab's tool set make cell wafers, logic foundries make periphery wafers, and wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding joins them (as CBA does for 3D NAND).
why: Capital and density: array-fab capex drops ~50%, die area per bit falls up to ~40% with periphery under the array, and each half runs on its optimal process.

title: No silicon: GaN-on-sapphire periphery from idle LED fabs
idea: Forced limit: no Si wafer for CMOS periphery. Idle LED MOCVD fabs grow AlGaN/GaN HEMT sense-amp and driver dies on sapphire (2DEG mobility about 1500 cm2/Vs), which are flip-bonded along the edges of glass oxide-TFT memory arrays.
why: Periphery is 49% of the die; putting it on fast GaN from stranded LED capacity lets cheap glass arrays reach about 50 ns access.

title: Offshore-wind contract-for-difference for new DRAM bits
idea: Adapted from UK offshore-wind CfDs: the government auctions 15-year contracts that pay new memory producers the gap between a strike price per Gb and a market index, and claws money back when prices exceed the strike.
why: Removes the boom-bust risk that blocks capex so new capacity can be financed at utility rates; in shortages like 2026 the clawback makes the net public cost near zero (capital intensity).

title: Gang-run press sheets: multi-project shuttles on a real DRAM line
idea: Commercial printers gang many small jobs onto one press sheet. A DRAM maker reserves a few wafers each month on which startups' and universities' novel cells, capacitors and periphery share one reticle field and run through the production capacitor module. Cost is split pro rata, as MOSIS/Europractice do for logic.
why: Innovation throughput and new entrants: cuts the cost of a real-process memory-cell trial from ~$20-50M (owning a line) to ~$0.2-0.5M, multiplying the number of credible new memory entrants.

title: Maskless laser interference lithography for periodic array gratings
idea: Po: light writes its own grating. A compact 193 nm (or 213 nm solid-state) multi-beam immersion interference exposure prints line/space and hex-dot gratings across the wafer with no mask and no projection lens; a cheap KrF/i-line step trims gratings into arrays and patterns periphery.
why: Interference tools are mostly lasers and prisms (~1/20 the cost of a scanner) yet reach the 30-40 nm pitches arrays need; attacks capital intensity and single-supplier risk.

title: Eliminate decommissioning: memory sleds outlive three CPU generations
idea: Eliminate the assumption that DRAM retires with its server: hyperscalers move bulk DDR into CXL-attached memory sleds on a 10-year depreciation schedule and swap only CPU/accelerator sleds every 3-4 years, inserting a retimer/protocol-bridge card at each refresh.
why: Fleet refresh scraps DIMMs at year 4-5 although bits last >10 years; decoupling cuts new-DRAM demand per refresh cycle ~30-50% with zero new wafers.

title: N: Cryo-binning resurrects retention-rejected DRAM dies in liquid nitrogen
idea: Dies and aging modules that fail 64 ms retention at 85 C because of the junction-leakage tail retain for seconds at 77 K; grade them by cold retention and sell them into LN2-cooled cold-memory sleds where refresh is nearly turned off.
why: Converts several percent of yield loss and retired modules into usable supply and cuts refresh energy >90% in that tier.

title: Spaghetti: printed hybrid CNT-read IGZO-write gain cells on foil
idea: Random stimulus 'spaghetti' -> tangled noodles as carbon nanotubes. Electrohydrodynamic-jet printing at ~1-2 um puts down a sol-gel IGZO write transistor (ultra-low leakage) and a sorted-CNT read transistor (high mobility, fast sensing) per cell on R2R foil, using US-made CNT inks.
why: A printable, vacuum-free capacity tier at est. <$1/GB process cost, offloading cold pages from DRAM; density is far below DRAM, so it serves as a far-memory tier.

title: Smackover brine bromine with closed-loop HBr recovery from scrubbers
idea: Combine Arkansas Smackover brine bromine production (a top U.S. resource) with wet-scrubber capture of HBr from etch exhaust. The scrubber liquor goes back to the brine plant for re-oxidation, making a closed domestic halogen loop for F-free silicon etch.
why: Secures a domestic, recyclable etch chemistry that cuts etch-gas cost and import exposure in an F-free fab.

title: Minify helium draw 20x with closed-loop fab recovery
idea: Fit membrane-plus-cryogenic helium recovery skids to wafer backside cooling, leak-check, etch and deposition exhausts, repurify to 6N on site, and recycle ~95% of helium.
why: Removes the Qatar chokepoint (~30% of supply, offline since March 2026) from DRAM output; helium becomes a top-up item, not a line-stopper.

title: W: Closed-loop WF6 recovery from CVD exhaust and target scrap
idea: Cryotrap unreacted WF6 from CVD exhaust (typical utilization 20-30%) and re-fluorinate tungsten chamber scrapings and sputter-target remnants back to WF6 in an on-site loop.
why: Cuts virgin tungsten demand ~50-70% in a supply chain ~80% controlled by China.

title: Tungsten embargo: WF6 exhaust recapture and closed-loop W recovery
idea: Self-imposed limit: no new tungsten imports. Cold-trap and sorbent modules on W-CVD exhaust capture unreacted WF6 for re-fluorination, and spent targets and chamber kits go to a hydrometallurgical W recovery loop at the fab.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: cuts virgin tungsten per wafer by about 50% or more and reduces exposure to the roughly 80% China supply share.

title: Par-baked wafers: import array-complete DRAM, finish in America
idea: Bakeries par-bake bread centrally and finish it in local ovens. Split the DRAM flow after the capacitor module. Array-complete wafers from an Asian partner ship to U.S. 'finishing fabs' that do the metal BEOL, fuse/repair, test, stacking and HBM base-die assembly on mostly mature, cheaper tools.
why: U.S. manufacturability: moves ~35-40% of value-add and all HBM assembly onshore in 18-24 months for <$3B, vs 5 years and $15B+ for a full fab.
